title: Three Buddhist Vocabularies: Computational Stylometry of the English Pali Canon across Sutta, Vinaya, and Abhidhamma

selection.evidence: NOTES: 'Read for two reasons: the Abhidhamma and the cetasikas are where my own essays live ... quantitative claims about the texts I care about.'

cost.compute_notes: arXiv PDF (16 pp) read in full. The paper's code/data are said to be released as extensions of the Darshana Graph corpus (arXiv:2606.18222); not located this session. Own null built from open sources: Brahmali's Theravada Vinaya translation AND notes from SuttaCentral bilara-data @ 10ad8c831fe5 (sparse checkout, translation/en/brahmali/vinaya + comment/en/brahmali/vinaya, ~11 MB, CC0) and four Project Gutenberg texts (50040, 2701, 731, 1404; sha256 in reanalysis/out/gutenberg_sha256.txt). Seconds to run.

claims.statement: The Mulasarvastivada Vinaya shares 20.0% vocabulary (Jaccard) and 49.1% (overlap coefficient) with the Theravada Vinaya, 'suggesting substantial shared legal heritage across two millennia of separate development'; the Dharmaguptaka (partial) shares 81.6% (overlap coefficient).
claims.scope: English translations: Brahmali 2026 (Theravada, PDF-extracted, 18,067 types) vs 84000 (Mulasarvastivada, 11,515 types) vs a 185-segment Dharmaguptaka rite (2,282 types); stopwords removed; point estimates, no baseline.

our_assessment.why: Decomposed 2026-11-12 (reanalysis/p2-p4), all as containment in Brahmali's Vinaya with notes (BTN, 15,170 types, bilara @10ad8c8), same tokenizer throughout. At about 9-11.5k types: English with no Buddhist connection reaches 0.31-0.34 (p1, Gutenberg); Buddhist non-Vinaya English reaches 0.46 (84000 house, p4, 8,903 types) to 0.48 (SuttaCentral house, Sujato, p2, 11,515 types); 84000's own Vinaya chapters reach 0.513 (p4). So of the ~0.5 the paper reads as 'shared legal heritage', ~0.33 is English, ~0.13 is Buddhist English, and ~0.05 is specific to the Vinaya: real (above the non-Vinaya 97.5th percentile; +0.06 at 2,282 types too) but a tenth of the number. Strongest alternative, untested: 84000's non-Vinaya texts are mostly Mahayana sutras, so part of the 0.05 may be mainstream-vs-Mahayana vocabulary rather than law. Corpus identity NOT established: 84000's five Vinayavastu chapters give 8,903 types (body), 14,456 (with notes), 17,486 (all TEI text); the paper reports 11,515, so its Mulasarvastivada corpus is not reproducible from what it describes. Earlier finding kept: the paper's Theravada Sutta (not a legal text) has a HIGHER overlap with the Theravada Vinaya (0.563) than the other school's Vinaya does, which is what a house-style account predicts and a heritage account does not.

claims.statement: Under MATTR-500 the Sutta and the Theravada Vinaya have nearly identical lexical diversity (0.399 vs 0.400), so their raw-TTR difference is a segmentation artefact; the Sangaha compendium is genuinely more diverse (0.560).
claims.scope: Sutta = Sujato's bilara-data translation segments; Vinaya = text extracted from Brahmali's PDF edition with pdftotext.

quantities.name: brahmali_vinaya_types_translation_only
quantities.baseline: with Brahmali's notes added: 15,170 types (notes alone 10,894 types in 56,570 tokens); paper's PDF extraction: 18,067 types

our_assessment.why: The paper handles segmentation well (MATTR, explicit caveats). It does not mention corpus composition. The Vinaya side was extracted from the PDF edition, which carries Brahmali's notes and front matter. In the bilara-data JSON the translation alone has 7,418 types; the notes add about 7,800 more. So roughly half of the 'Vinaya vocabulary' is a modern scholar's English apparatus. The Sutta side has no notes (bilara segments). Every type-based comparison across the two -- TTR, Jaccard, overlap, translation shift -- therefore compares a translation with a translation-plus-commentary. MATTR on the token stream is less affected, but the notes are ~11% of tokens in a register more diverse than the translation. Whether the 0.399/0.400 equality survives a notes-free Vinaya is untested here (the paper's PDF corpus is not in hand).

relations.why: Same shape in a different field: a similarity number is read as a substantive relation (shared heritage) without the baseline that any two texts of the same language and register already achieve.

open_questions: ANSWERED 2026-11-12 (p2-p4): Buddhist non-Vinaya English already reaches 0.46-0.48 of the ~0.5; the Vinaya-specific excess, same translation house, same size, is +0.05 (+0.06 at 2,282 types). See c1. Notes-free Brahmali (BT) gives the same ordering, about 0.03 lower throughout.
Locate the Darshana Graph release (arXiv:2606.18222) and check whether its Vinaya corpus includes notes.

Pali-original version: overlap of Pali vocabularies (Theravada Vinaya vs the Sanskrit/Tibetan-derived parallels) would remove the translator layer entirely; needs aligned parallels (SuttaCentral has parallel tables).

Is the remaining +0.05 law, or mainstream (sravaka) vs Mahayana vocabulary? Rerun p4 with a non-Vinaya null restricted to 84000's sravaka-style sutras (agama parallels in the Kangyur), if enough are translated to reach ~9k types.

Which corpus gives the paper's 11,515 Mulasarvastivada types? Not the five 84000 Vinayavastu chapters under any extraction tried (8,903 / 14,456 / 17,486). Ask the author, or locate the Darshana Graph release (open question 2).
